notes.title: TechFlow SOC 2 Type II — engagement status
notes.content:
Reporting period 1 January to 31 December 2026. Fieldwork substantially complete.

Open: change management (CC8.1) — evidence requested 20 February, partially supplied. Access re-certification (CC6.2) — no evidence of a formal quarterly review; this will be an exception unless something arrives.

Two exceptions likely. Neither is disqualifying but both will appear in the report and relying parties will read them.

notes.title: Evidence outstanding — TechFlow
notes.content:
CC8.1: need branch protection configuration showing author-cannot-merge, plus a sample of ten changes with reviewer identity.
CC6.2: need evidence of at least one completed access review in the period. There is not one.

I have asked three times. I cannot tell them how to fix it, only what the control requires — and the difference between those two sentences is my independence.

notes.title: Why I will not advise on remediation
notes.content:
Every client asks. The answer is always the same.

I can tell you what a control requires and what evidence satisfies it. I cannot tell you how to design your process, because then I would be testing my own work.

Firms that blur this get their reports discounted by the parties relying on them, which defeats the purpose of having one.

notes.title: Relying party enquiries
notes.content:
Kestrel's security engineer has asked for the report. That is normal and correct — once issued, the audited entity authorises distribution and I send it.

He also asked whether there were exceptions, before issuance. I declined. A finding in progress is not a finding, and telling a relying party about one early would change how the audited entity behaves toward me.

notes.title: Report timing
notes.content:
Draft to management for response by 15 April. Management response two weeks. Issuance late April or early May.

Anyone who needs the report before a decision gate in April is not going to have it.

notes.title: Engagement portfolio
notes.content:
Nine SOC 2 engagements this year, three of them Type II with December year ends.

December year ends mean fieldwork in January and February, which is why the first quarter is unrecoverable.

notes.title: Common exceptions — the top three
notes.content:
Access review not performed or not evidenced. Change management with no evidence of independent approval. Termination access not removed within policy.

Those three account for most exceptions in this practice. None is difficult; all are boring and therefore skipped.

notes.title: Type I versus Type II
notes.content:
Type I is design at a point in time. Type II is operating effectiveness over a period.

Clients ask for Type I to get a report fast and are surprised their customers do not accept it. Their customers are right.

notes.title: Evidence collection — what makes it slow
notes.content:
Not the volume, the format. A screenshot without a timestamp or a system identifier is not evidence, and roughly a third of first submissions are exactly that.

I publish the format requirements up front and it does not seem to help.

notes.title: Independence — the hardest conversation
notes.content:
Every client wants advice and I cannot give it. The line is that I can state what a control requires and cannot design their process.

Firms that blur it get their reports discounted, which defeats the purpose of having one, which I say to every client at kickoff.

notes.title: Complementary user entity controls
notes.content:
The section nobody reads. It says which controls the customer has to operate for the report to mean anything.

Relying parties routinely accept a report and ignore the section that tells them what they still have to do.

notes.title: Report distribution
notes.content:
The audited entity authorises recipients. I do not decide who gets it.

Relying parties sometimes come to me directly. The answer is to ask their vendor.

notes.title: Subservice organisations
notes.content:
Carve-out or inclusive. Most choose carve-out, which pushes the question one layer down and is often where the actual risk sits.

A carve-out is honest. It is also a place to hide, and the two look identical in a report.

notes.title: Practice utilisation
notes.content:
Chargeable running above target, which sounds good and means fieldwork quality is under pressure.

Raised it. The response was to congratulate me on utilisation.

notes.title: Continuing education
notes.content: Forty hours. Mostly framework updates, which change slowly, and one course on emerging areas, which changes fast and is where the interesting work will be.

notes.title: What clients get wrong about scope
notes.content:
The trust services criteria selected determine the report. Security is mandatory; availability, confidentiality, processing integrity and privacy are optional.

A client who selects only security and then tells customers they are 'SOC 2 certified' is overstating, and it is very common.

notes.title: The five trust services criteria
notes.content: Security is mandatory. Availability, confidentiality, processing integrity and privacy are elected. Most clients elect security and confidentiality and are surprised how much privacy adds.

notes.title: Common exceptions across the book
notes.content: Access reviews not performed, change management evidence incomplete, and vendor management existing only as a spreadsheet. Same three every year across every client.

notes.title: Sampling methodology
notes.content: Population, frequency, and risk determine sample size. Clients believe the sample is negotiable. It is not, and explaining why takes longer than pulling it.

notes.title: Management response — what makes a good one
notes.content: An exception with a management response that names an owner and a date reads completely differently to a relying party than one that says the control has since been improved.

notes.title: Independence — the annual attestation
notes.content: Firm-wide. No financial interest, no operational involvement, no advising on what we test. It is checked and it is the thing that makes the report worth anything.

notes.title: Peer review — the firm's own
notes.content: Triennial. Ours is next year. Auditors being audited concentrates the mind in a way that is good for everyone.

notes.title: Why I will not tell you how to fix it
notes.content: If I design the control and then test it, I am testing my own work and the report is worth nothing to the party relying on it. Every client asks, usually kindly, and the answer never changes.

notes.title: Scheduling — the busy season
notes.content: December through March is fieldwork for calendar-year clients. Everything else compresses around it.
